about: How the example's agent traces each idea down: what it answers, and what it rests on, down to first principles (crates/core/src/foundations.txt). An idea not here rests on nothing.

Retries.question: What do you do when a call fails for a reason that might pass?
restsOn: Transient errors
A retry can only help with a failure that passes.
Idempotence
Trying again is safe only if doing it twice does no more than once.
usedWith: A timeout ends a hung call, so the retry around it can start.
alternatives: Stop calling a service that keeps failing, instead of trying it again.

Transient errors.question: Which failures pass on their own?
restsOn: Partial failure
A transient error is part of a system failing for a while, while the rest goes on.

Exponential backoff.question: How long should a client wait before trying again?
restsOn: Retries
It sets how long to wait between them.
Exponential growth
Each wait is a fixed multiple of the last.
answers: Waiting longer each time lowers the load on a service that is struggling.
usedWith: Jitter picks a random wait below the ceiling backoff sets.
alternatives: Stop calling for a while instead of calling less often.

Jitter.question: Why add randomness to when clients retry?
restsOn: Randomness
A wait chosen at random can't line up with anyone else's.
answers: Spreads out clients that would all come back at the same moment.
usedWith: Sets the ceiling jitter picks under.
alternatives: The server refuses what it can't take, instead of clients spreading out.

Randomness.question: What makes a choice random?
usedWith: A computer's random numbers come from a rule that only looks random.

Pseudorandomness.question: How does a computer make numbers that look random?
restsOn: Randomness
It imitates the lack of pattern a random sequence has.

Thundering herd problem.question: What goes wrong when many waiting processes wake at once?
restsOn: Network congestion
Everything arriving at once is more load than the service can take.

Network congestion.question: What happens when a service gets more load than it can carry?
restsOn: Bandwidth
Congestion is more load than a link's bandwidth can carry.

Exponential growth.question: What grows by a fixed multiple each step?
restsOn: Arithmetic
Each step multiplies the last by the same amount.

Idempotency keys.question: How can a request sent twice be carried out once?
restsOn: Idempotence
The key makes repeating a request idempotent.
Unique keys
The service remembers each key once, and refuses it twice.
usedWith: A retry sends the same key again, so it can't do the work twice.

Idempotence.question: Which operations can be repeated safely?
restsOn: State
Doing it again leaves the state where the first time left it.
Function
An idempotent function gives the same result applied once or twice.

Timeouts.question: How long should a caller wait for an answer?
restsOn: Partial failure
A call can fail by never answering, which only a time limit can tell.
Time and clocks
A limit needs a clock to measure the wait against.
alternatives: Watch a service's health instead of guessing a time limit.

Authorisation holds.question: How do you take money only once a payment is settled?
restsOn: Double-entry bookkeeping
Holding money is moving it to a held account and back.
Two-phase commit
First every side agrees, then the change is made.

Two-phase commit.question: How do several parties agree to make a change together?
restsOn: Atomicity
The change happens everywhere, or nowhere.
Partial failure
Any party can fail midway, so each first says it can commit.

Double-entry bookkeeping.question: How do you keep books that always balance?
restsOn: Accounting equation
Each entry keeps both sides of the equation equal.
usedWith: Both entries are written together, or not at all.

Accounting equation.question: What must always be true of a set of accounts?
restsOn: Arithmetic
Its two sides are sums that must always be equal.

Database transactions.question: How do several changes to a database happen all at once, or not at all?
restsOn: Atomicity
A transaction's changes happen together or not at all.
usedWith: A lock taken in a transaction is let go when it ends.

Atomicity.question: What does it mean for a change to be indivisible?
restsOn: State
Others see the state before the change or after it, never between.

Advisory locks.question: How can a program lock something the database doesn't know about?
restsOn: Mutual exclusion
Only one holder of the lock goes on at a time.
usedWith: A transaction-scoped lock is let go when the transaction ends.

Mutual exclusion.question: How do you stop two things changing the same thing at once?
restsOn: Concurrency
It's needed only when things run at the same time.
State
Two changes at once can leave shared state inconsistent.

HMAC.question: How do you prove who sent a message, with a secret you share?
restsOn: Hash function
The code is a hash of the message mixed with the secret.
Secret
Only those who share the secret can make the code.
usedWith: Checking a code must not leak, through its timing, how much of it matched.

Constant-time comparison.question: How do you compare secrets without leaking them through time?
restsOn: Secret
It keeps a secret from leaking through how long a check takes.
answers: Taking the same time whatever the input leaves nothing to measure.

Timing attacks.question: How can the time something takes give a secret away?
restsOn: Measurement
The attacker measures how long each answer takes.
Secret
What leaks is a secret the system meant to keep.

Unique keys.question: How does a database keep two rows from sharing a value?
restsOn: Identifier
A unique key identifies one row and no other.

Probability.question: How do we measure how likely something is?

State.question: What does a system remember from one moment to the next?

Circuit breakers.question: How do you stop calling a service that keeps failing?
restsOn: Partial failure
It notices one part failing and stops sending it work for a while.

Rate limiting.question: How does a service refuse more than it can take?
restsOn: Network congestion
It turns load away before the service is overwhelmed.

definitions.Idempotence: Doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once.
definitions.Circuit breakers: Stopping calls to a service that keeps failing, for a while.
definitions.Partial failure: Part of a system failing while the rest goes on.
definitions.Exponential growth: Growth by the same multiple each step.
definitions.Network congestion: A service or link given more load than it can carry.
definitions.Randomness: Having no pattern anyone can use to predict it.
definitions.Thundering herd problem: Many waiting processes woken at once for something only one can have.
definitions.Rate limiting: A service refusing requests beyond a set rate.
definitions.Pseudorandomness: Numbers from a rule that only look random.
definitions.Probability: How likely something is, as a number from 0 to 1.
definitions.Arithmetic: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing numbers.
definitions.State: What a system remembers from one moment to the next.
definitions.Function: A rule that gives one output for each input.
definitions.Time and clocks: Measuring time, and agreeing on it across machines.
definitions.Unique keys: A rule that no two rows of a table may share a value.
definitions.Two-phase commit: Asking every party first, then telling all of them to make a change.
definitions.Atomicity: A change that happens whole, or not at all.
definitions.Accounting equation: Assets equal liabilities plus equity, always.
definitions.Mutual exclusion: Only one thing at a time in the part that touches a shared resource.
definitions.Concurrency: Several things running at the same time.
definitions.Hash function: A function from any data to a short, fixed-size value.
definitions.Secret: Something only those meant to know it know.
definitions.Timing attacks: Learning a secret from how long a system takes to answer.
definitions.Measurement: Finding a quantity by comparing it with a standard.
definitions.Identifier: A name or number that picks out one thing.
definitions.Bandwidth: How much a link can carry in a given time.
definitions.Database transactions: A group of changes to a database made together, or not at all.
definitions.Double-entry bookkeeping: Recording every movement of money twice: as it leaves an account, and as it arrives.
definitions.Advisory locks: A lock a program names and the database keeps.
definitions.Retries: Trying a failed call again, in the hope it works the next time.
definitions.Transient errors: Failures that pass on their own, so trying again can work.
definitions.Exponential backoff: Waiting longer after each failure, each wait a multiple of the last.
definitions.Jitter: A random amount taken from a wait, so many clients don't act at the same moment.
definitions.Timeouts: Giving up on a call that takes too long, so the caller can move on.
definitions.Constant-time comparison: Comparing secrets in a way that takes the same time whatever they hold.
